title: How to Go Vegetarian (or Vegan) Without Falling Off in Week Two
summary: The failure points are predictable: protein, convenience and social friction. Here is the plan that fixes all three.
body:
Most people who quit a vegetarian diet do so in the first 30 days, and the reasons are boringly consistent: they feel hungry, they run out of easy meals, and they get tired of explaining themselves. None of those are nutrition problems. They are systems problems, and systems can be designed.

1. Decide what 'vegetarian' means for you

Lacto-ovo (dairy and eggs stay), lacto, ovo, pescatarian, flexitarian, or fully plant-based. Pick one and write it down. Ambiguity is where cravings live.

2. Fix protein first

Aim for roughly 1.2–1.6 g of protein per kilogram of body weight if you are active. Anchor every meal on one of: tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans, seitan, edamame, Greek-style soy yogurt, or a protein shake. Use the AllVeg protein calculator to get your number.

3. Build a five-meal rotation

You do not need 200 recipes. You need five dinners you can cook without a recipe. Start with chana masala, lentil bolognese, black bean tacos, teriyaki tempeh bowls and Thai green curry.

4. Stock the pantry once

Canned chickpeas, black beans, lentils, coconut milk, crushed tomatoes, soy sauce, nutritional yeast, tahini, peanut butter, rice, pasta and frozen vegetables. With these you are never more than 10 minutes from dinner.

5. Supplement B12. Non-negotiable.

Vegans need a B12 supplement (25–100 µg daily or 1000 µg twice weekly). Vegetarians eating dairy and eggs usually get enough but many still supplement. Vitamin D in winter and omega-3 (algae oil) are sensible additions.

6. Script the social moment

Have one sentence ready: 'I eat plant-based most of the time — I'm easy, I'll find something.' Then change the subject. Nobody wants a lecture, including you.

title: The Complete Vegetarian Protein Guide (With a Table You'll Actually Use)
summary: Grams per serving for 30 plant foods, how much you need, and the three mistakes that keep vegetarians under-muscled.
body:
Protein is the first question every vegetarian gets asked and the one most of us answer badly. Here is the data.

How much do you need?

  • Sedentary adult: 0.8 g/kg body weight
  • Active / recreational training: 1.2–1.6 g/kg
  • Strength athletes or fat loss: 1.6–2.2 g/kg

A 70 kg person training three times a week needs about 100 g/day. That is entirely achievable on plants, but not by accident.

Protein per serving

FoodServingProtein
Seitan100 g25 g
Tempeh100 g20 g
Firm tofu150 g18 g
Lentils, cooked1 cup18 g
Edamame1 cup17 g
Chickpeas, cooked1 cup15 g
Black beans, cooked1 cup15 g
Greek yogurt170 g17 g
Cottage cheese½ cup14 g
Paneer100 g18 g
Eggs2 large12 g
Soy milk1 cup8 g
Quinoa, cooked1 cup8 g
Peanut butter2 tbsp8 g
Hemp seeds3 tbsp10 g
Pea protein powder1 scoop24 g

The three mistakes

1. Replacing meat with carbs. Pasta with tomato sauce is a vegetarian meal with 8 g of protein. Add a cup of lentils and it is 26 g.

2. Ignoring leucine. Soy, lentils and pea protein are leucine-rich and trigger muscle synthesis; spread 25–40 g protein across 3–4 meals rather than one big dinner.

3. Fearing soy. Decades of human trials show normal soy intake (1–3 servings a day) has no effect on testosterone or estrogen in men and is associated with lower breast-cancer risk in women.

title: We Tested 7 Vegan Egg Substitutes in Real Baking. Here's What Works.
summary: Flax, chia, banana, applesauce, aquafaba, silken tofu and commercial replacer — each baked into the same muffin recipe.
body:
We baked one control muffin recipe seven times, changing only the egg replacement. Rise, crumb, moisture and taste were scored blind by four people.

Results

SubstituteRatioRiseCrumbVerdict
Flax egg1 tbsp + 3 tbsp waterGoodSlightly dense, nuttyBest all-rounder for muffins and cookies
Chia egg1 tbsp + 3 tbsp waterGoodDense, visible specksGreat in brownies; specks show in light bakes
Mashed banana¼ cupFairMoist, gummy edgesOnly where banana flavour is welcome
Applesauce¼ cupFairVery moistBest for cakes; add ¼ tsp extra baking powder
Aquafaba3 tbspExcellentLight, openWinner for anything that needs lift
Silken tofu¼ cup blendedFairRich, custardyIdeal for dense, rich bakes and quiche
Commercial replacerPer packGoodNeutralReliable, costs more

Rules of thumb

  • Recipes with 1–2 eggs substitute easily; 3+ eggs usually need a purpose-built vegan recipe.
  • For binding (burgers, meatballs): flax or chia.
  • For lift (sponge, meringue): aquafaba.
  • For richness (custard, cheesecake): silken tofu.

title: B12, Iron, Omega-3, Calcium: The 4 Nutrients Vegetarians Must Plan For
summary: What the evidence says, how much you need, and the cheapest way to get each one.
body:
A well-planned vegetarian diet is associated with lower rates of heart disease, type-2 diabetes and several cancers. 'Well-planned' does the heavy lifting in that sentence. Four nutrients need a plan.

Vitamin B12

No reliable plant sources exist. Vegans: supplement 25–100 µg daily or 1,000 µg 2–3× weekly. Lacto-ovo vegetarians: dairy and eggs supply some, but testing every couple of years and supplementing is prudent. Deficiency damage to nerves can be permanent — this is the one non-negotiable.

Iron

Plant (non-haem) iron absorbs at 5–12% versus 15–35% for haem iron, so vegetarians need roughly 1.8× the RDA: about 32 mg/day for menstruating women, 14 mg for men. Pair iron foods (lentils, tofu, pumpkin seeds, spinach, fortified cereal) with vitamin C, and keep tea and coffee an hour away from meals — tannins cut absorption by up to 60%.

Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)

Flax, chia and walnuts supply ALA, which converts to EPA/DHA at only 5–10%. An algae-oil supplement of 250–500 mg EPA+DHA daily closes the gap at the source fish get it from.

Calcium

1,000 mg/day. Calcium-set tofu (look for calcium sulphate on the label), fortified plant milk (300 mg/cup), tahini, kale and bok choy. Spinach's calcium is mostly bound to oxalate — count it as zero.

Also worth watching

Vitamin D (everyone, in winter), zinc (legumes, seeds, soak/sprout to improve absorption), iodine (iodised salt or seaweed).

This is general education, not medical advice. If you have a condition or are pregnant, get bloodwork and speak with a registered dietitian.

title: Best Plant-Based Protein Powders in 2026: Tested for Taste, Mixability and Protein per Dollar
summary: Pea, soy, hemp, rice and blends — how they score on the metrics that matter, and which one wins for most people.
body:
We rank by four criteria: protein per serving, leucine content, cost per 20 g protein, and blind taste in water and soy milk.

What to look for

  • Pea + rice blends give a complete amino-acid profile with ≥2 g leucine per scoop.
  • Soy isolate is the cheapest complete protein and mixes cleanest.
  • Hemp tastes earthy and delivers only ~15 g per scoop — better as a food than a supplement.
  • Ignore 'superfood blends' — they add cost, not protein.
  • Check for third-party testing (Informed Sport, NSF) if you compete.

title: Eating Out Vegetarian: A City-by-City Cheat Sheet and the 12 Chains That Are Reliably Safe
summary: What to order at the chains everyone has, plus quick guides for the most-searched cities.
body:
Searches for 'vegan restaurants near me' outnumber 'vegan recipes' six to one. Here is the practical version.

Chains with dependable veg options

  • Chipotle — sofritas bowl (20 g protein).
  • Taco Bell — anything 'fresco style', bean burrito.
  • Panera — Mediterranean veggie sandwich, ten-vegetable soup.
  • Subway — veggie delite with plant patty where offered.
  • Starbucks — impossible sandwich, oatmeal, soy/oat milk.
  • Pizza chains — most doughs are vegan; ask for no cheese or vegan cheese.
  • Indian, Thai, Ethiopian, Middle Eastern restaurants — a third to half of the menu is typically vegetarian by default.

title: Raising Vegetarian Kids: What Paediatric Dietitians Actually Recommend
summary: Growth, iron, B12 and picky eating — the evidence-based version, without the alarmism.
body:
The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets are healthful for all life stages, including infancy and childhood. The word 'planned' matters more for children than adults because of their energy density needs.

Energy density

Small stomachs, high needs. Include calorie-dense foods at every meal: nut butters, avocado, tahini, full-fat soy milk, olive oil on vegetables.

Iron & zinc

Lentils, beans, tofu, fortified cereals, pumpkin seeds, with a vitamin-C food alongside. Limit milk (any kind) to ~500 ml a day so it does not displace iron-rich foods.

B12

Vegan children need a supplement — full stop. Fortified foods alone are unreliable at their intake volumes.

Protein

Rarely a problem if calories are adequate: 1 cup soy milk + ½ cup lentils + 2 tbsp peanut butter already exceeds a 6-year-old's daily requirement.

Picky eating tactics that work

  • Serve the new food beside a known favourite, 10–15 exposures.
  • Kids eat what they help cook — start with banana pancakes and energy balls.
  • Blend vegetables into sauces (lentil bolognese hides a lot).
Educational content only. For infants under 12 months or any growth concern, consult a paediatrician or registered dietitian.

title: Vegan Cheese Explained: Which Ones Melt, Which Ones Don't, and How to Make Your Own
summary: Cashew, coconut-oil, potato-starch and cultured cheeses compared, plus a 15-minute nacho sauce.
body:
'Vegan cheese' is at least four different products. Knowing which is which saves you from a rubbery pizza.

The four types

  • Coconut-oil + starch shreds — melt and stretch well; flavour is mild. Best for pizza, grilled cheese.
  • Cashew-based — rich, tangy, do not melt; best as spreads, sauces and cheesecake.
  • Cultured nut cheeses — aged like dairy cheese, complex flavour, premium price. Cheese boards.
  • Nutritional-yeast sauces — cheap, cheesy flavour, pourable. Mac and cheese, nachos.

15-minute nacho cheese sauce

  1. Boil 1 cup diced potato and ½ cup carrot until soft.
  2. Blend with ¼ cup nutritional yeast, 3 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp salt, ½ tsp paprika and ½ cup of the cooking water until silky.

title: Vegetarian & Vegan Diets in Numbers: Health, Environment and Cost (2026 Data)
summary: The headline statistics — from cardiovascular risk to greenhouse-gas emissions to the size of the plant-based market — with sources.
body:
Facts to hand for the next dinner-table debate.

Health

  • Vegetarian diets are associated with ~25% lower ischaemic heart disease mortality in pooled cohort analyses.
  • Type-2 diabetes prevalence is roughly half in vegans versus non-vegetarians in the Adventist Health Study-2.
  • Average BMI runs 1–2 points lower in vegetarians in large cohorts.

Environment

  • Animal agriculture accounts for roughly 14.5% of global greenhouse-gas emissions (FAO).
  • Producing 100 g of beef protein emits ~50 kg CO₂e versus ~1 kg for 100 g of pea protein (Poore & Nemecek, 2018).
  • A plant-based diet uses about 75% less farmland than a diet high in meat.

Market

  • The global vegan food market is estimated at $22–25 billion in 2025–26, growing ~11% a year (Grand View Research).
  • 'Vegan' draws ~550,000 US searches a month; 'vegan restaurants' ~300,000.

Figures are rounded from the cited studies and reports; consult primary sources for precise values.
